 New Tennessee vehicle registration law takes effect Jan. 1
 Find out what paperwork Moore County motorists will need before heading to the County Clerk's office for a tag
 11:20 a.m. Nov. 20, 2026
 DUANE CROSS
 MCO Publisher•Editor 
 Buying a car or truck next year? If the transaction requires a new Tennessee license plate, you'll need documentation showing you're legally in the United States before the county clerk can process the registration.
 Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Tennessee law will require applicants seeking an initial motor vehicle registration involving the issuance of a license plate to establish U.S. citizenship, lawful permanent residency or temporary presence authorized by the federal government.
 The requirement comes from Tennessee Code Annotated § 55-4-144, enacted by the General Assembly earlier this year as part of Public Chapter 954. It prohibits county clerks from processing qualifying registration applications without the required documentation and applies statewide, including at the Moore County Clerk's office.
 For most Tennessee drivers, the necessary proof is probably already in their wallet. A valid Tennessee driver's license satisfies the requirement, even if it isn't REAL ID-compliant. Tennessee photo IDs and temporary licenses also qualify, along with REAL ID-compliant licenses.
 What documents will you need?
 Motorists without one of those accepted licenses or identification cards have other options.
 U.S. citizens may establish their status with an official birth certificate, valid U.S. passport, certificate of naturalization or certificate of citizenship. Lawful permanent residents may present a Permanent Resident Card, commonly called a green card, or certain other federal immigration documents.
 People legally in the country on a temporary basis may use a valid foreign passport accompanied by the appropriate visa and federal arrival records. Additional paperwork may be necessary depending on immigration status.
 The law also allows applicants to present documentation electronically, including images displayed on a cellphone or another portable device.
 The usual paperwork still applies
 Proving citizenship or lawful presence is only part of the registration process. Tennessee's existing identification and residency requirements remain in place.
 Applicants must provide one primary identification document or two secondary documents, along with qualifying proof of residency. Utility bills, bank statements, rental agreements and Tennessee voter registrations are among the documents the state accepts.
 Residency requires two documents from the state's primary list, or one primary and one secondary document.
 Moore County residents registering a new vehicle must also provide the manufacturer's statement of origin and vehicle invoice. Used vehicles require a properly assigned title and an odometer disclosure statement when applicable.
 People moving to Tennessee from another state should bring their current out-of-state registration and lienholder information, if applicable. Those without that information must provide their out-of-state title.
 The new requirement also applies when a dealership handles a qualifying registration for a customer. Dealers must submit a copy of the buyer's required documentation with the application.
 What about registration renewals?
 Tennessee motorists won't have to prove their citizenship every time they renew their tags. The new documentation requirement applies to initial registrations involving the issuance of a license plate, not routine annual renewals. Once the state has recorded an applicant's qualifying documentation, that person is considered compliant unless otherwise required by law.
 Motorists will, however, see a new notice accompanying vehicle registrations and renewals. It states that vehicle owners or operators must be U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents or temporary lawful residents under the statute. The notice does not impose a new annual documentation requirement.
 The Tennessee Department of Revenue maintains the complete requirements and acceptable-document lists on its vehicle registration website .
 Anyone relying on documents other than an accepted driver's license or state-issued ID should check the state's requirements before making a trip to the Moore County Clerk's office.
